basis: Independently curated original deck retained in full, with original note-based additions reviewed against the subject specification. External notes supply coverage prompts, not verbatim cards.

base_cards.front: Name the magnetic material commonly used as a transformer core.
back: Iron.

base_cards.front: What happens when two north poles are brought together?
back: They repel.

base_cards.front: What is the unit of magnetic flux density?
back: Tesla (T).

base_cards.front: Which device uses the generator effect to convert sound vibrations into an electrical signal?
back: A microphone.

base_cards.front: Name the effect that makes a current-carrying coil move in a loudspeaker.
back: The motor effect.

base_cards.front: Does a stationary magnet beside a stationary coil produce a sustained induced potential difference?
back: No.

base_cards.front: What does the north-seeking end of a compass show?
back: The direction of the local magnetic field.

base_cards.front: Which ring arrangement connects a simple alternator coil to its external circuit?
back: Two slip rings.

base_cards.front: Distinguish a permanent magnet from an induced magnet.
back: A permanent magnet **retains its magnetism** and produces its own field.
An induced magnet becomes magnetic in an external field and usually **loses most or all magnetism when the field is removed**.

base_cards.front: Why does attraction alone not prove that an iron object is a permanent magnet?
back: An initially unmagnetised iron object can become an **induced magnet**.
It is then **attracted** to the magnet, even though it was not a permanent magnet.

base_cards.front: Give two changes that increase the strength of an electromagnet.
back: Increase the **current** through its coil.
Add an **iron core** or increase turns per unit length.

base_cards.front: Describe the field inside a long solenoid, away from its ends.
back: It is **strong and approximately uniform**.
Draw **parallel, evenly spaced** field lines with the same direction.

base_cards.front: Why is a compass needed as well as iron filings when mapping a magnetic field?
back: Filings show the field’s **pattern**.
A compass shows its **direction**, using the north-seeking end of its needle.

base_cards.front: State the directions shown by Fleming’s first finger and second finger.
back: First finger: **magnetic field**, from north to south.
Second finger: **conventional current**, positive to negative.

base_cards.front: A wire carries 4.0 A perpendicular to a 0.20 T field. A length of 0.15 m is within the field. Calculate the force.
What happens to the force on a wire if only the current is reversed? What if both current and field reverse?
back: Reversing current alone **reverses force**.
Reversing both leaves force in its **original direction**.

base_cards.front: Explain why a split-ring commutator is used in a simple DC motor.
back: It **reverses current in the coil every half-turn**.
This reverses the side forces at the appropriate position, keeping the **turning effect in the same rotational direction**.

base_cards.front: A magnet is moved into a coil connected to a voltmeter. Give two ways to increase the peak induced potential difference.
back: Move the magnet **faster**.
Use a **stronger magnet** or more turns in the coil, with otherwise comparable conditions.

base_cards.front: Why can a voltmeter show induced potential difference even when the coil does not carry a significant current?
back: A changing linked field induces **potential difference across the coil**.
A substantial current requires a **complete conducting circuit**; potential difference does not require current to flow.

base_cards.front: What happens to the induced signal if a magnet moves out of a coil instead of into it? Explain the comparison.
back: Its **polarity reverses** for the same pole orientation.
The field change is reversed. Magnitude depends on speed and the other conditions.

base_cards.front: Explain why a transformer normally needs AC rather than steady DC.
back: AC creates a **continuously changing magnetic field** in the core.
This induces secondary potential difference. Steady DC does not provide the sustained field change needed.

base_cards.front: Why is iron suitable for a transformer core?
back: It is **easily magnetised**.
Its magnetisation can change and reverse with the **alternating primary current**, linking the changing field to the secondary.

base_cards.front: A transformer has 500 primary turns and 100 secondary turns. Is it step-up or step-down? Explain.
back: **Step-down**.
Fewer secondary turns mean **lower secondary potential difference**.

base_cards.front: Explain how a moving-coil loudspeaker makes sound.
back: Changing current flows in a coil within a magnetic field, producing a **changing motor-effect force**.
The attached coil and cone **vibrate** as the current changes.
The cone creates **pressure variations in air**, producing sound waves.

base_cards.front: Explain how a moving-coil microphone makes an electrical signal.
back: Sound pressure variations **vibrate a diaphragm and attached coil**.
The coil moves in a magnetic field, changing the field linked with it.
The **generator effect induces a changing potential difference** that represents the sound.

base_cards.front: A perpendicular wire experiences a 0.018 N force in a 60 mT field while carrying 2.0 A. Calculate the length within the field.
A transformer has 300 primary turns at 240 V and 30 secondary turns. Calculate secondary voltage and state the type.
back: **Vₛ = Vₚ × nₛ/nₚ**.
It is **step-down**.

base_cards.front: Explain how AC in a primary coil leads to potential difference in a secondary coil.
back: AC makes a **changing magnetic field** around the primary.
The iron core links the changing field with the secondary.
This **induces alternating potential difference** across the secondary.

base_cards.front: Explain how an induced current opposes a magnet being pushed into a coil.
back: Movement changes the magnetic field linked with the coil and induces current.
The current produces a field that **opposes the original change**.
An opposing magnetic force means **work must be done** to continue pushing, supplying the electrical energy.

base_cards.front: Compare the potential-difference graphs of a simple alternator and a simple dynamo.
back: Alternator **AC crosses zero**, changing sign each half-turn.
Dynamo output remains in **one external direction** because the split ring swaps connections.
Its output can **pulse**, so DC does not necessarily mean constant size.

base_cards.front: An ideal transformer supplies 18 V at 2.0 A from a 240 V source. Calculate primary current.
back: Secondary power = VₛIₛ = 18 × 2.0 = **36 W**.
Ideal primary power = secondary power.

base_cards.front: For the same transmitted power, a grid voltage is doubled. State the new current and heating loss as fractions of their original values, with resistance fixed.
back: P = VI, so current becomes **one half**.
Cable heating follows **I²R**.
Heating loss becomes (1/2)² = **one quarter**.

base_cards.front: Describe a compass method for plotting the field around a bar magnet.
back: Trace the magnet on paper and keep it fixed.
Place a small compass nearby and mark both ends of its needle.
Move it to continue from a previous mark, repeating to trace a line. Join marks smoothly.
Add arrows using the **north-seeking end** and repeat from other starting points. Keep other magnetic objects away.

base_cards.front: An 80% efficient transformer supplies 12 V at 3.0 A from a 240 V source. Calculate input power and input current.
back: Output power = 12 × 3.0 = **36 W**.
Efficiency = output/input, so input power = 36/0.80 = **45 W**.
Input power exceeds output because some energy is dissipated.

base_cards.front: Explain how opposite forces on the two sides of a motor coil can cause rotation rather than canceling the turning effect.
back: The sides carry current in **opposite directions** within the same field.
They experience opposite motor-effect forces.
The forces act at **different positions** and create moments in the same rotational sense.
In a simple DC motor, a split-ring commutator reverses coil current each half-turn to maintain rotation.

additions.front: What does a dot mean for current viewed end-on?
back: Conventional current coming out of the page.

additions.front: What field direction surrounds current coming out of the page?
back: Anticlockwise, using the right-hand grip rule.

additions.front: What field direction surrounds current going into the page?
back: Clockwise.

additions.front: Why does the solenoid grip rule follow current around the turns?
back: The wire carries current around the coil, while the thumb gives its axial field and north-pole direction.

additions.front: What happens when a magnet is held still inside a stationary coil?
back: There is no sustained induced potential difference because the linked field is not changing.

additions.front: How does pulling a north pole out compare with pushing it in?
back: It reverses the induced polarity when the meter connections are unchanged.

additions.front: Why can swapping meter leads complicate induction comparisons?
back: It reverses the displayed sign independently of the magnet’s movement.

additions.front: What usually happens to an induction pulse when the same motion is faster?
back: It becomes larger and briefer.

additions.front: Does a stronger generator field at unchanged rotation speed increase frequency?
back: No. It increases peak potential difference; rotation rate determines cycle frequency.

additions.front: How does a louder same-pitch sound affect a microphone signal?
back: It generally increases signal amplitude without changing frequency.

additions.front: What output comes from 240 V with 600 primary and 150 secondary turns?
What ideal input current supplies 60 V at 2.0 A from a 240 V primary?
back: 0.50 A, since power is 120 W on both sides.

additions.front: Why cannot an ideal transformer increase both voltage and current by the same factor?
back: Their product is power, which must be conserved.

additions.front: Why keep current fixed when comparing solenoid turns?
back: Otherwise a change in field strength could be caused by current as well as turn count.
